The A18 Pro MacBook is likely to arrive within the next few weeks, and while everyone is discussing it's possible performance, RAM, etc, there's one crucial piece of the puzzle most people are missing: power usage, and therefore battery life.

Apple Silicon (ARM) is very efficiency in its own right, which is what has set it apart from traditional X86 processors. However, while the M-Series chips sip power and provide outstanding performance per watt, in power draw alone they don't beat the A-Series processors. This isn't a surprise, lower performance for mobile/tablet devices = less required wattage.

As silicon advancements progress, higher performance can be achieved at the same wattage. This is mostly made possibly by node shrinks, which involves shirking the size of the chips transistors. The benefits of this are two fold: 1. Smaller transistors require less power to operate and 2. There is more room to fit in additional transistors, which is what allows the performance to be increased while keeping the same power draw.

When the M1 chip first released, the equivalent A-Series chip at the time was the A14, a 5nm (the measurement used to measure the size of the transistors\*) chip. As you'd except, it was much less powerful than the higher wattage M1.

Fast forward to the release of the A18 Pro, now on a 3nm process. It draws \~10W maximum power, and around \~3-4W idle, while now having the same performance as an M1, and sometimes slightly better (considerably better in single core). For comparison, the M1 draws \~7W at idle and \~39W maximum\*\*!

On the device that the A18 Pro was designed for, an iPhone 16 Pro, the battery capacity is 13.94wh, providing around \~14 hours of screen on time\*\*\*. This is tiny compared to laptop batteries, with the 13in MacBook Air having a capacity of 53.8wh. So if we're to be very conservative and say the A18 Pro MacBook has a battery size 50% smaller than the MacBook Air, we're looking at 26.9wh, while is still considerably larger than the iPhone battery.

How much of a difference is that? The 16 Pro Max has 18 hours of screen on time using the same testing conditions with a battery size of 18.17wh, a 4 hour difference compared to the 16 Pro. Using that logic\*\*\*\*, there is 0.9456wh for each hour of battery life. Applying that to our conservative estimation figure for the size of the A18 Pro MacBook battery, and we're looking at around 26 hours of screen on time. Factoring in the larger screen, keyboard, trackpad, and other additional components, we're are likely still looking at over 20 hours of battery life\*\*\*\*\*. I highly doubt that the battery will be as small as this, unless they want to make the thinnest and lightest laptop ever made (which would also be quite cool), so in reality, it'll probably be even more.

we're are likely still looking at over 20 hours of battery life\*\*\*\*\*. I highly doubt that the battery will be as small as this, unless they want to make the thinnest and lightest laptop ever made (which would also be quite cool), so in reality, it'll probably be even more. This is going be a major unique selling point for this device, against many rivals. Windows laptops at the same price obviously won't be able to keep up in both performance and battery life, which is the case with Apple Silicon in general anyway, however the difference will be especially evident this time because of the incredibly low wattage of the A18 Pro, even compared to M-Series. Drawing off of that, people looking to buy a MacBook Air who don't require the extra power of an M4/M5 chip may be drawn to this budget MacBook because of its stronger battery life (the air gets around 10-13 hours of screen on time, task dependent\*\*\*\*\*\*).

Overall this is much more exciting device than people are making it out to be, and with the same, premium aluminium finish as on the rest of the range as confirmed by Gurman, this has the opportunity to be one of the best "netbooks" available. If we do manage to get that $599 price point, we might be looking at a $499 sale MacBook in the near future.

**---Disclamers/Information---**

\*The actual size of the transistors are not 5 nano metres / 3 nano metres (etc) - it's more of a marketing term these days. However, a 3nm chip still has smaller transistors than a 5nm chip, just not the size quoted.

\*\*[M1 (Mac Mini) power usage statistics. ](https://support.apple.com/en-gb/103253)

\*\*\*[iPhone 16 Pro / Pro Max battery test source.](https://www.tomsguide.com/phones/iphones/iphone-16-battery-life-results-are-in-and-we-can-hardly-believe-our-eyes) Note that your mileage may vary considerably depending on what tasks you're doing.

\*\*\*\*Wh = 18.17 - 13.94 = 4.23 Wh  
Hours = 18 - 14 = 4 hours  
Rate = 4 hours / 4.23Wh = 0.9456 hours per Wh

\*\*\*\*\*I don't have an accurate way of measuring this so I can't be entirely sure about this figure.

\*\*\*\*\*\*[MacBook Air battery test source.](https://www.wired.com/review/macbook-air-13-inch-2025/) Note that your mileage may vary considerably depending on what tasks you're doing.

You've hit the nail on the head with all of these points. It's funny you post this, because I recently tried to make the switch to a Galaxy S25 Ultra but ended up returning it and going back to my iPhone. And I'm not even someone deep in the Apple ecosystem I use a Windows PC and the only other Apple product I own is a pair of AirPods.
While I agree with all your criticisms of iOS, there were several dealbreakers on the Android side that made me switch back:

* Password Managers: The autofill experience on Android is, frankly, terrible. I use both 1Password and Proton Pass, and it's a constant gamble whether the autofill prompt will even appear. When it does, it often only fills one field, leaving me to copy and paste the rest manually. It's miles behind the seamless integration on iOS.

* Face ID vs. Fingerprint Scanner: For me, Face ID is simply superior. I have very dry hands, and the ultrasonic fingerprint scanner was a frustrating experience, with about a 70% success rate. I'd have to try multiple times or just give up and type my PIN. Face ID just works, every single time, without me having to think about it.

* Push Notifications: Android's aggressive battery optimization is a major headache. Out of the box, it will kill background processes to save power, which means I was constantly missing important notifications. The only way to fix it is to manually go into the battery settings for every single app and set them to "unrestricted," which is something a user shouldn't have to do for core functionality.

* Software Bloat & Duplicate Services (Samsung): The sheer number of redundant apps and services was confusing. Should I use Google backup or Samsung's backup? Photos backed up to Google Photos or OneDrive, which is integrated into the Samsung Gallery? It felt like I had two of everything, creating a cluttered and less streamlined experience.

* App Optimization: It's a cliché at this point, but apps just feel more fluid and polished on iOS. There's a level of consistency and optimization that Android still seems to be chasing.

So, while I'm still incredibly annoyed by the issues you mentioned, the fundamental user experience on iOS is more reliable for me.

Hey everyone. So my contract is finally up and I'm due for an upgrade. I've been an Android person for years but some of my friends keep trying to convert me to iPhone. With both the new Samsung and Apple flagships out now, I'm really stuck trying to figure out the Samsung Galaxy S26 vs iPhone 17 Pro situation.

I've watched some YouTube videos and read a few articles but honestly the comparisons all sound like marketing copy. I want real talk from people who've used both or follow this stuff closely. The S26 just launched at Unpacked a couple days ago and the iPhone 17 Pro has been out since September . Both seem great on paper but I know real world is different.

For context, I use my phone for everything. Social media, some light photo editing, watching videos, and I play Genshin Impact sometimes. Battery life is huge for me because I'm bad about charging overnight. Camera matters but I'm not a professional or anything.

From what I've gathered, the S26 has a 6.3-inch display with peak brightness around 3000 nits . The iPhone 17 Pro is also 6.3 inches with similar brightness claims . Both have 120Hz screens now which is good. The iPhone has that anti-reflective coating that sounds nice for outdoor use .

Chipwise it's complicated. US models of the S26 get the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, other regions get the Exynos 2600 . iPhone has the A19 Pro . Some early benchmarks show the S26 Ultra beating the iPhone 17 Pro Max in multi-core scores by like 18%, and single-core is finally catching up . But I know real world feel matters more than numbers.

Battery seems close. S26 reportedly has 4,300 mAh, iPhone has 4,252 mAh in eSIM models . But charging is where it's different. iPhone supports 40W wired and 25W wireless, while Samsung is still at 25W wired and 15W wireless . That's actually kind of disappointing if true.

Cameras are another story. S26 has a 50MP main with a new 50MP ultrawide upgrade, but keeps the 10MP telephoto with 3x zoom . iPhone 17 Pro has all 48MP sensors across main, ultrawide, and telephoto, with 4x optical zoom . That telephoto difference seems significant.

Price wise, iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1099 . Samsung is expected to keep the S26 at $799 to compete with the base iPhone 17, but the Pro model is obviously higher .

For people who've actually used both or follow this stuff:

In the Samsung Galaxy S26 vs iPhone 17 Pro battle, which handles everyday tasks smoother? I've heard iOS is more optimized but Android has come a long way.

How's the battery life in real world? The specs are close but I know software optimization matters more.

For someone coming from Android, is switching to iPhone worth the hassle of learning a new system?

After more than 30 years as a Windows user, I finally made the switch to macbook, and honestly… I don’t see myself going back. Here is quick review of my apple devices

MacBook Air M4

This thing has been amazing. Everything feels smooth, intuitive, and just works without me constantly troubleshooting. macOS feels cleaner and less stressful than what I was used to on Windows. For daily use, it’s been a great experience.

Apple Watch SE 2

Does exactly what I need it to do. Sleep tracking, fitness, basic health stuff — nothing fancy, but reliable and simple. No complaints here.

iPhone 16 Pro

Overall a much better experience than my android devices i had over the years , but  I’m a bit disappointed. Since i updated to iOS 26, it feels like things went downhill for me:

•	Battery life is noticeably worse

•	Camera photos look more washed out than before

Still a great phone to use , just not as impressive as my experience with ios 18

AirPods Pro 2

So I don’t think it makes much sense for anyone to go out and buy the M3 Pro MacBook Pro. Either spend the same amount of money on the base M4 MacBook Pro or spend way less on an M1 Pro MacBook Pro. That, I think, is the best decision if you’re in the market for a MacBook Pro.

7. Air or Pro?

Now to the question of whether you should buy a MacBook Air or MacBook Pro. I think for 90+% of people, the Air is the correct choice. I absolutely could have gotten by using a MacBook Air. The new MacBook Airs with Apple silicon are super powerful machines, and for the overwhelming majority of people who are just doing everyday tasks like surfing the web, streaming videos, checking email, doing normal work tasks like writing documents and working with spreadsheets, and even some light video and photo editing, the base MacBook Air is a great option, especially since Apple just upgraded the Air to start at 16 GB of memory standard. Obviously, if you’re doing more intensive work like serious photo or video editing or working with graphics-intensive tasks like 3D modeling, then of course the Pro makes more sense. But I’m going to avoid focusing on that group of people because for the most part, they know who they are and the kind of device they need. But when it comes to the everyday user (like myself), I think the Pro does make sense for a select group. First, if you want the best laptop display, the displays on the Pros are noticeably better than the Airs. Now, this is absolutely not to say that the Air has a bad display; it absolutely does not, and it’s still a great display. But if you’re a bit of a display snob like me, it may make sense to spend a bit more on the Pro, even if like me you aren’t engaged in super demanding tasks on a regular basis. Another consideration more geared towards everyday people is the port selection. The MacBook Pros come with 3 Thunderbolt USB-C ports compared to the 2 that come on the Air. This is a big deal not just because it’s nice to have the extra port, but because this enables you to charge the laptop from either side which is super convenient when you need to charge but the outlet is on your right. The Pro also comes with an HDMI port and an SD card slot. These extra ports can make a huge difference even if you’re just a student and need to plug your laptop into a display in the library, which I frequently do. It’s super nice to have that HDMI port and not have to remember to bring an adapter. The MacBook Pro isn’t just for professionals; it’s for those who want a more premium laptop experience and are willing to pay for it.
